# Interpretation notes (auto-generated by R/07_interpret.R)

Facts for the Discussion section. Every number is computed from the saved
models and the tables in `outputs/tables/`. Do not edit by hand.

## Feature importance (T06, F18)

- Random-forest ranking: 1. g − r (%IncMSE 52.0); 2. u − g (%IncMSE 13.9); 3. r − i (%IncMSE 9.9); 4. r (mag) (%IncMSE 7.7); 5. i − z (%IncMSE 5.5).
- Most important feature: g − r (random forest), g − r (largest |standardised coefficient| in the linear model).
- r magnitude: RF rank 4 of 5; LM coefficient 0.0080 [95% CI 0.0028, 0.0132]: positive, so fainter galaxies are predicted at higher z, as the inverse-square law expects.
- u − g: almost no correlation with z on its own (training r = 0.06) but RF rank 2 and LM coefficient -0.0344 [-0.0431, -0.0257] at fixed g − r. Interpretation: u − g traces galaxy type (old/red vs star-forming/blue), which lets the models tell an intrinsically red galaxy from one reddened by redshift in g − r.
- The colours are strongly correlated with each other (F05), so individual
  linear coefficients can trade off against each other; their CIs are wide.

## Hypotheses (README §3.6)

- **H1** (g − r is the most important predictor): **supported** by both RF and LM.
- **H2** (predicted z rises monotonically with g − r): **supported**. Spearman ρ of the RF partial-dependence curve = 0.98 (threshold 0.8).
- **H3** (non-linear models beat linear regression): CV **partly supported** (only M4 SVR beat LM); test **partly supported** (only M2 k-NN, M3 Random Forest beat LM). CV RMSE: LM 0.0238, k-NN 0.0324, RF 0.0302, SVR 0.0217. Test RMSE: LM 0.0418, k-NN 0.0376, RF 0.0318, SVR 0.0444.
- **H4** (all models beat the mean baseline): CV **supported**, test **supported** (point estimates; baseline CV 0.0440, test 0.0457). The test CIs in T05 overlap the baseline for 3 of 4 learners.

## Physics of the sample

- Test galaxies with at least one feature outside the training range: 2 of 20.
- Negative (unphysical) test predictions: 2 (M1 Linear, M4 SVR). Linear and kernel models can extrapolate beyond the training redshifts; random-forest predictions are averages of training redshifts and cannot.
- Over this sample's redshift range (0.025–0.221) the 4000 Å break stays inside the g band (F20), so the redshift signal is the break moving *within* g, which reddens g − r.
